facts.fact: The World Bank states that the MVRS project, which followed in 2011 and ran with UNICEF support over 2013-2015, computerised the birth registration process, and that death registration, though provided for in the MVRS software, was not made operational; URSB annual reports for 2013-14 to 2015-16 give 2,030,355 births registered.

The World Bank states that MVRS used web-based transmission of data and mobile phone messaging to computerise birth registration, digitising data recording and transmission at connected ('online') registration points whose activity could be seen centrally; it dates this to the project period 2011-2015.

The World Bank states that MVRS had 202 connected registration points, a modest portion of the more than 1,400 sub-counties and 345 health facilities (as of July 2012) where registration was possible, and was reportedly installed in 77 districts (NIRA and Plan International 2017); the count itself is not dated, so the end of the project period is used.

The World Bank reports the MVRS registrations from the annual reports of the Uganda Registration Services Bureau, which managed all civil registration from 2004 until the transfer to NIRA on 1 January 2016.
The World Bank describes MVRS as a UNICEF-supported project, implemented over 2013-2015, and gives no domestic budget line for it; URSB annual reports give no separate civil registration expenditure.

The World Bank states that the civil register consisted, and under the 2015 law still consists, of the manually made, paper-based registers kept by registrars across the country (more than 10 million records), beside about 3-5 million entries in the digital systems MVRS and CRIMS; the diagnostic was made between November 2017 and June 2018.
facts.system: civil register for births and deaths

facts.fact: The World Bank states that responsibility for birth, death and adoption registration passed from URSB to the National Identification and Registration Authority on 1 January 2016, under the Registration of Persons Act 2015.
facts.system: civil register for births and deaths

facts.fact: The World Bank cites NIRA's Strategic Plan 2017/18-2019/20, subtitled as scaling up civil registration and vital statistics, with a budget of USh 624.2 billion over three years, and adds that a costed national CRVS strategic plan will also be critical; it does not say the plan names a registration system.
facts.system: civil register for births and deaths

facts.fact: The World Bank states that the Government of Uganda, the World Bank, UNICEF and Plan International cover half of NIRA's planned USh 624.2 billion for 2017/18-2019/20, that the medium-term allocation is USh 269 billion (43 per cent of the need), and that the Bank's Reproductive, Maternal and Child Health Services Improvement Project is funding NIRA to scale up birth and death registration; the budget covers the national ID as well as civil registration.
facts.system: civil register for births and deaths
